An abreaction is the sudden, intense release of emotions that were locked up inside a person — emotions that were originally tied to a painful or traumatic memory that they had buried deep in their mind, often without realizing it.

Think of it like a pressure cooker. When a traumatic event happens, sometimes the mind cannot handle the full emotional weight of it, so it pushes that memory — along with all the painful feelings attached to it — down into the unconscious mind (the part of the mind you don't have direct access to). But those trapped emotions don't disappear. They sit there under pressure. An abreaction is what happens when that pressure finally escapes — when the emotions burst out, usually because the buried memory is brought back to the surface.

Where this concept comes from

Abreaction is a term from psychoanalysis — the field of psychology that studies the unconscious mind and how hidden thoughts and feelings shape our behavior. The concept was developed in the late 19th century and is closely linked to how therapists understand and treat trauma — deeply distressing experiences like accidents, abuse, war, loss, or any event that overwhelms a person's ability to cope.

The core idea: repression

To truly understand abreaction, you first need to understand repression.

When something terrible happens to a person, the mind sometimes protects itself by pushing the memory of that event out of conscious awareness. This is called repression. The person might not even consciously remember the event, or they may remember it vaguely but feel emotionally "numb" about it — as if it happened to someone else. The memory is there, but it's been buried.

The critical thing is this: the emotions that belong to that memory get buried along with it. The grief, the fear, the anger, the shame — they get locked away, unprocessed and unexpressed.

What happens to those trapped emotions?

Here's the problem. Repressing a memory doesn't neutralize those emotions — it just hides them. They continue to exert pressure from the unconscious mind. This is why people who have experienced trauma often develop symptoms that seem unconnected to their past — anxiety, unexplained physical pain, sudden mood swings, nightmares, or emotional numbness. The buried emotional energy has to go somewhere, and it leaks out in these indirect ways.

So what is an abreaction, exactly?

An abreaction is the discharge of that buried emotional energy — the moment when the feelings that were trapped inside the traumatic memory finally get released. This typically happens when the person is brought back into contact with the buried memory, and as a result, they re-experience the emotions attached to it — sometimes with great intensity.

During an abreaction, a person might:

  • Cry deeply or sob uncontrollably
  • Shake or tremble
  • Feel a sudden rush of rage or fear
  • Scream or gasp
  • Physically relive sensations from the original event

It is not just remembering a painful event. It is re-experiencing the emotional storm of it — feeling it fully, perhaps for the very first time, because the original repression prevented them from fully processing it when it actually happened.

How does an abreaction happen?

In therapy: Abreaction most commonly occurs during psychological therapy, particularly trauma therapy. A therapist might gently guide a patient to revisit a painful memory — through conversation, guided imagery, hypnotherapy, or methods like EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing). As the patient makes contact with the buried memory, the emotions tied to it rise to the surface and are released. This release — that intense emotional outpouring — is the abreaction.

Spontaneously, outside therapy: Abreactions can also happen without any therapeutic setting. A specific smell, a piece of music, a location, a photograph, or even a tone of voice can act as a trigger — something that unconsciously connects to the buried memory. Suddenly, a person might find themselves overwhelmed by emotion seemingly "out of nowhere." That is an abreaction being triggered by an external cue.

Is an abreaction the same as catharsis?

These two words are closely related, and people often use them interchangeably, but there is a meaningful distinction.

Catharsis is the broader term — it simply means an emotional release that brings relief. You can experience catharsis from watching a sad movie, listening to music that moves you, or having a good cry after a hard week. It doesn't require a repressed memory.

Abreaction is more specific. It refers particularly to the emotional release that is tied to a repressed traumatic memory. Every abreaction is a kind of catharsis, but not every catharsis is an abreaction. Abreaction happens specifically in the context of trauma and repression — it is catharsis with a specific psychological mechanism behind it.

Does an abreaction heal a person?

The early theory — developed by Freud and his colleague Josef Breuer — was that abreaction was itself the cure. By allowing the trapped emotional energy to discharge, the symptoms caused by repression would dissolve. This was called cathartic therapy.

Modern understanding is more nuanced. Abreaction is now seen as an important part of the healing process, but not the whole of it. Simply releasing the emotions is not always enough — the person also needs to make sense of the memory, integrate it into their understanding of their life, and develop a healthier relationship with it. An abreaction without proper therapeutic support can sometimes be overwhelming or even retraumatizing rather than healing.

That said, abreaction remains a recognized and significant event in trauma therapy. It is often a turning point — a sign that a deeply buried experience is finally being processed.
A Clear Example to Bring It All Together

Imagine a woman named Sarah who, as a child, witnessed a house fire that killed her pet and terrified her deeply. Her young mind couldn't cope with the trauma, so she repressed it. She grew up with no clear memory of the event, but she developed an unexplained intense fear of the smell of smoke, anxiety that she couldn't account for, and occasional nightmares.

Years later, in therapy, her therapist carefully helps her revisit some childhood memories. As Sarah begins to approach the memory of the fire, she suddenly starts sobbing uncontrollably — she feels the fear of that night flooding through her body, her heart races, she trembles, and she cries in a way she hasn't cried in decades.

That moment — that powerful, full-bodied outpouring of emotion tied to the long-buried traumatic memory — is an abreaction. The emotional pressure that had been locked inside for years has finally found a way out.

To put it as plainly as possible: an abreaction is the release of repressed emotional pain connected to a buried traumatic memory — a sudden, intense emotional discharge that happens when that buried memory is brought back into conscious awareness. It is a concept rooted in trauma psychology, it can happen in therapy or be triggered spontaneously, and it is often an important (though not sufficient on its own) part of healing from trauma.
